summary: Defines a connection-less variant of the Lightweight Directory Access Protocol, using single datagrams to reach the X.500 Directory without the resource cost of the full Directory Access Protocol. It is now historic and was replaced by RFC 3352.

eli5.summary: Instead of a long phone call to ask a directory a question, you send a quick postcard and get a postcard back.

subtitle: A faster way to query the directory using single datagrams instead of multiple connection-oriented exchanges.

tldr.problem: The full Directory Access Protocol requires many network exchanges and resource overhead. Simple directory lookups do not need all this machinery.
tldr.mechanism: CLDAP sends requests and responses as single UDP datagrams, reusing much of LDAP's design but eliminating connection setup, teardown, and session overhead.
tldr.outcome: Lookups complete in a few datagrams instead of a dozen. It is Historic and was replaced by RFC 3352.

today: RFC 3352 obsoletes this protocol. CLDAP is not widely deployed; the X.500 Directory itself has given way to LDAP and DNS for directory services.

sections.title: The Problem with Connection-Oriented Lookup
sections.content:
The full Directory Access Protocol (DAP) connects to the X.500 Directory by setting up multiple layers of session and presentation connections, binding to the directory, performing the lookup, unbinding, and disconnecting. For simple lookups—such as finding a peer's network address from its name—this takes about 10 network packets and can take several seconds.

CLDAP (Connectionless Lightweight Directory Access Protocol) eliminates this overhead. It sends requests and responses as single UDP datagrams, much like DNS. For a simple lookup, the total is just 4 packets, or 2 if the server caches results or co-locates with the directory.
sections.eli5: Asking a phone operator for a number is slow; looking it up in a phonebook is fast. CLDAP is the phonebook method.

sections.title: The CLDAP Design
sections.content:
CLDAP inherits most of its structure from LDAP but strips away connection overhead. It runs directly over UDP or other connectionless transport. A client sends a request describing what to look up (the search request), and the server returns one or more response datagrams with the results. Unlike LDAP, there is no login step, no persistent connection, and no explicit disconnect.

Clients must handle the unreliability of UDP by retrying requests with exponential backoff if no response arrives within a timeout. This is the same retry logic that DNS resolvers use.
sections.eli5: You send a postcard asking a question and listen for the answer. If you don't hear back, you send it again and wait longer.

sections.title: Messages and Errors
sections.content:
A CLDAP request is a single message with a message ID, the user's name, and a search request (which comes from LDAP). The response is one or more messages containing the entries found. An encoding optimisation lets a response refer to the base object's name with just a star character instead of the full name, saving bytes in typical cases.

CLDAP adds one new error code: resultsTooLarge (70), which the server returns when the response would not fit in a single UDP datagram. The client must then either try a simpler search, ask the server to continue the search, or use a more capable protocol like DAP.
sections.eli5: The message is a postcard: a question number, your name, and what you want to know. The answer fits on another postcard, or the server says 'the answer is too long for a postcard.'

sections.title: Deployment Guidance
sections.content:
Servers should stay bound to the Directory during idle periods or remain bound permanently to avoid reconnect delays when a CLDAP request arrives. Caching results is highly desirable but must be balanced against the lack of a cache invalidation protocol in DAP. If the CLDAP protocol is implemented directly in a directory server, these issues disappear.

Clients should use a retry algorithm similar to DNS stub resolvers, locating servers by IP address rather than domain name when possible to avoid recursive lookups. The specification does not mandate a specific retry timing, only that clients implement backoff to avoid network storms.
sections.eli5: The server should remember recent answers and be ready to respond right away. The client should keep trying with longer pauses if the postcard doesn't come back.

sections.title: Security Trade-Offs
sections.content:
CLDAP provides no authentication facilities. The design trades security for speed and simplicity. Servers are expected to bind to the Directory anonymously or with simple authentication. Applications that need authenticated access to the Directory should use the full Directory Access Protocol instead.

The lack of authentication means CLDAP is suited only for public directory data or within trusted networks. The single-datagram nature also rules out encryption during the exchange itself, though encryption of the transport layer (such as secure UDP) would be an addition outside this protocol.
sections.eli5: Anyone can ask questions and get answers. If you need secrets, use a more secure protocol.
